claims.text: Conventionally processed W particles or connected W regions in a Cu matrix exhibit interfacial heterogeneity and void or defect issues.
SPS provides rapid heating and cooling and permits microstructural control.
Machine-learning optimization can identify SPS temperature gradients, ramp rates, and cooling times suitable for W–Cu processing.
The optimized SPS schedule will enhance W–Cu interfacial bonding and diffusion without melting W.
The proposed SPS regime can keep Cu near or in its molten state while W remains solid.
Optimized rapid heating and controlled cooling will create a refined, defect-free W–Cu interfacial diffusion layer.
The refined interface will minimize voids and phase separation.
An ML model trained on vapor-coated sintered samples and other SPS experiments can predict an optimal W–Cu processing window.
The predicted processing window promotes atomic interdiffusion and oxide-layer removal at the W–Cu interface.
SPS can produce a composite with a uniform distribution of reinforcement in a matrix.
ML-optimized SPS will produce a more uniform W–Cu composite with fewer voids than vapor-coated sintering.
Lower void density and better interfacial continuity will improve W–Cu thermal conductivity.
The ML-optimized composite will maintain or improve mechanical strength and durability under irradiation.
Vapor-coated W powders sintered as the baseline achieve near-perfect contact between W and Cu.
The vapor-coated sintered baseline nevertheless retains phase inhomogeneity and defect-related limitations.
SPS temperature control can prevent W melting and Cu boiling during the proposed process.
The resulting material is applicable to high-thermal-flux, irradiation-exposed fusion-reactor joints.
Failure to obtain statistically significant reductions in void density and improvements in both thermal conductivity and mechanical durability relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
